title: Incremental Latency Regression During Region Failover - Postmortem Draft
body:
Summary:

On 2026-03-10 at ~03:15 UTC customers began reporting elevated tail latencies and intermittent streaming disconnects for the Hosted API in the eu-west-1 region. Impact increased gradually over ~45 minutes and peaked at 04:05 UTC with a 95th-percentile latency increase from baseline 110ms to ~1.4s and a ~8% increase in streaming session failures. Traffic was automatically routed to the eu-west-2 standby as part of a regional failover initiated by the infra control plane due to a partial network flap. The failover itself completed, but we observed a persistent, incremental latency regression on eu-west-2 over the following hour that correlated with increased KV-cache miss rates and growing inference queue lengths on leader nodes.

Customer impact:
- Degraded token generation latencies across the Hosted API (95p from ~110ms to ~1.4s).
- Streaming connections saw higher error rates and occasional aborts; estimated affected requests ~6–10% of regional traffic during the peak window.
- No data loss; responses were eventually served or failed with 5xx in a small fraction (<0.5%) attributed to overloaded worker processes.
- Major customers on SLAs saw latency SLO breaches; paging occurred.

Detection and alerting:
- Primary detection: user-reported Slack channel + elevated 95th/99th percentiles in latency dashboard auto-alerts at 03:42 UTC.
- Secondary detection: increase in request queue length alert and KV cache miss-rate anomaly at 03:48 UTC.
- Existing runbook suggested immediate rollback to previous routing but did not account for cache warmup state after failover.

Timeline (UTC):
- 03:10: Partial network flap in eu-west-1 detected by infra telemetry; control plane begins automated region failover.
- 03:15: Traffic shift starts toward eu-west-2; initial routing succeeds and failures are low.
- 03:30: Latency 95p starts climbing; early symptoms recorded but below paging thresholds.
- 03:42: SRE on-call alerted by latency SLO monitor; engineers start investigation.
- 03:48: KV cache miss-rate rises 6x baseline; queue length increases on a subset of inference pools.
- 03:55: Streaming disconnects spike; on-call opens incident channel and begins mitigation.
- 04:00: Traffic throttling and temporary increase in worker pool size attempted; partial improvement.
- 04:05: Peak latency observed (~1.4s 95p); decision made to enable aggressive KV cache prefill and reduce per-request batching window to prioritize latency.
- 04:30: Latency gradually improves but remains above baseline until 05:15 when cache hit rates returned to normal.

Root cause:
Primary: During automated region failover, traffic was shifted to eu-west-2 without a coordinated KV-cache warmup and pre-provisioning of inference leaders for the increased load. The control plane created new routing entries that pointed to warm standby nodes which had much lower cache residency (KV entries for common prefixes and persona-based cached policy data were cold). This caused a higher proportion of requests to require full KV lookup + model KV population, increasing per-request work and raising CPU/GPU scheduling contention and queue lengths.

Contributing factors:
- Runbook gap: failover playbook did not mandate cache prefill or staged traffic ramp steps for multi-tenant inference caches.
- Batching policy: default continuous-batching window was tuned for throughput; when cache misses increased, batches expanded to hold more tokens which increased end-to-end latency for tails.
- Leader provisioning: auto-scaling was slow to allocate leader processes for certain model families due to a conservative cooldown setting.
- Observability blind spot: cache-residency heatmaps were available in dashboards but not wired to automated pre-failover checks or runbook triggers.

Mitigations performed during incident:
- Increased worker pool target and lowered autoscaler cooldown (temporary override) to bring more leaders online (04:00–04:20 UTC).
- Temporarily reduced batching window from 30ms to 10ms for high-latency routes to prioritize latency over throughput (04:05 UTC).
- Triggered aggressive KV-cache prefill for the most-used prefixes via a scripted warmup from synthetic clients (04:10 UTC).
- Applied temporary routing policy to drain the coldest standby nodes and prefer nodes with >60% cache residency (04:15 UTC).

Why mitigations took time:
- Cache prefill needed to generate realistic request prefixes to populate model KV; warmup rate limited by rate limits and risk of noisy neighbor impact.
- Autoscaler cooldown prevented instant leader spin-up; required manual override.

Post-incident permanent fixes planned:
1) Failover runbook update (owner: Jing Wu, due 2026-03-18): add explicit cache-warmup stage, staged traffic ramping (10%->33%->100%) and pre-provision leader pools.
2) Observability alert (owner: Devon Reed, due 2026-03-12): wire KV-cache-residency heatmap to an automated pre-failover check that blocks full cutover until minimal cache residency is met or an operator acknowledges.
3) Autoscaler tuning (owner: Liam O'Connor, due 2026-03-20): reduce leader cooldown during failover and add a fast-path for emergency scaling.
4) Batching policy improvement (owner: Aisha Patel, due 2026-03-25): add adaptive batching profile that shortens window on cache-miss spikes and high tail latency.
5) Synthetic warmup tooling (owner: María Torres, due 2026-03-22): build safe prefill tooling that can populate KV cache at controlled rates per-tenant.

Runbook and playbook changes (summary):
- Add new "Region Failover -> Cache Warmup" subsection with step-by-step actions, safety checks, and automation idempotency guards.
- Document staged traffic ramp percentages and automatic verification metrics (cache hit-rate, leader CPU/GPU utilization, queue depth) required before advancing stage.
- Add explicit abort criteria and rollback path if queue depth or 99p latency rises beyond thresholds during ramp.

Action items (short):
- "Jing Wu: Update failover runbook and get review from SRE and Serving Runtime (due 2026-03-18)"
- "Devon Reed: Create pre-failover automation check for KV-cache residency and add dashboard panel (due 2026-03-12)"
- "Liam O'Connor: Implement autoscaler fast-path + reduced cooldown for leader pools (due 2026-03-20)"
- "María Torres: Deliver synthetic cache-warmup tool with tenant rate-limiting (due 2026-03-22)"
- "Aisha Patel: Add adaptive batching mode and test in staging (due 2026-03-25)"

Metrics to monitor post-fix:
- KV-cache residency by model family and tenant (target >70% within 30 minutes of failover).
- 95/99p latency pre and post staged cutover.
- Queue depth distribution across leader nodes.
- Streaming session error-rate during and post-failover.

Lessons learned:
- Failovers are more than routing; stateful caches and runtime warm state must be first-class considerations for multi-region inference platforms.
- Automation should include safety gates that verify application-level state (cache residency) before moving to full traffic cutover.
- Adaptive runtime policies (batching, autoscaling) need tuning to handle transient spikes in per-request work.

Appendix — On-call notes (raw):
- "03:42: saw 95p tick up; pulled up cache panels, saw miss-rate climbing but didn't initially connect to failover. Note to self: cross-check region routing events earlier next time."
- "03:55: tried adding workers; autoscaler cooldown blocked immediate scale. Need fast escalation path to override."
- "04:08: warmup script helped; after 20 mins saw hit-rate recover and latency fall. Synthetic prefill effective but must be throttled."

Appendix — Quick postmortem summary for customers (one-paragraph):
On 2026-03-10 we observed increased latency and intermittent streaming failures in the eu-west Hosted API during an automated region failover. The root cause was a cold application-level KV cache on the failover target which increased per-request work and induced queueing. We executed mitigations (temporary scaling, cache prefill, batching adjustments) and fully recovered by 05:15 UTC. Permanent fixes are planned to ensure cache warmup and staged traffic ramping on future failovers.

Open questions for follow-up:
- Do we want an automated pre-warm path for every failover or only for specific model families?
- Can we expose cache residency guarantees to customers (transparency vs. implementation complexity)?
- What limits do we put on synthetic prefill to avoid noisy neighbor issues?
